citations.quote:
Let $\omega>0$ and $T:=2\pi/\omega>0$.

**Scalar form.** Let $a,d\in\mathbb C$. Then

$$\frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}\bigl(ae^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\operatorname{Re}\bigl(de^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}\bigl(a\overline d\bigr).$$

**Vector forms.** Let $a,d\in\mathbb C^3$, write the same symbols for the componentwise complex-bilinear extensions of the Euclidean inner product and of the cross product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] to $\mathbb C^3$, and let $\operatorname{Re}$ act componentwise. In coordinate formulas, $\epsilon_{ijk}$ is $+1$ for even permutations of $(1,2,3)$, $-1$ for odd permutations and zero for repeated indices; all displayed repeated-index sums run from 1 to 3. Then

$$\frac1T\int_0^T\bigl\langle\operatorname{Re}\bigl(ae^{-i\omega t}\bigr),\operatorname{Re}\bigl(de^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\bigr\rangle\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\langle a,\overline d\rangle\bigr),\qquad \frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}\bigl(ae^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\times\operatorname{Re}\bigl(de^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}\bigl(a\times\overline d\bigr),$$

the integrals of the real vector-valued integrands being componentwise. The real-valued functions $\operatorname{Re}(ae^{-i\omega t})$ are the time-dependent factors of the plane-wave fields of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]] at a fixed position, with the phase absorbed into $a$ and $d$; no electromagnetic interpretation is asserted. Real quadratic expressions may not be replaced by complex quadratic expressions without conjugation: the average is not $\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(ad)$ in general. For $a=d=1+i$ the proved average is $\tfrac12|1+i|^2=1$, whereas $\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}((1+i)^2)=0$.

Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], so
that $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a nonempty open interval, $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$
is nonempty open, $x=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ is the position in the spatial chart,
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the frame basis of the spatial slice, and the spatial inner
product is the Euclidean form $\delta$; let the units and the constants $c>0$,
$\mu_0>0$ and $\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ be those of
[[def-em-si-conventions]]; let $k\ge1$, and let
$E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be an electric and a magnetic field of class
$C^k$ of [[def-em-fields]]. Write $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ and $|\cdot|$ for
the Euclidean inner product and norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and
$\times$ for the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].

(a) [Energy density and flux] The **electromagnetic energy density**
$u:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ and the **energy flux density** (the **Poynting
vector**) $S:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ are defined by

$$u(x,t):=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\,\langle E(x,t),E(x,t)\rangle+\frac{1}{2\mu_0}\,\langle B(x,t),B(x,t)\rangle,\qquad S(x,t):=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\,E(x,t)\times B(x,t).$$

At fixed $t\in I$ the map $u(\cdot,t):\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is a real-valued
function on $\Omega$ and $S(\cdot,t):\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ is a spatial vector
field on $\Omega$, read in the basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. The energy density
carries $\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}=\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-1}\mathrm s^{-2}$ and
the energy flux density carries $\mathrm W\,\mathrm m^{-2}=\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm s^{-3}$.

(b) [Regularity] If $E,B$ are of class $C^k$, then $u$ and $S$ are of class
$C^k$: they are the components of a polynomial expression in the components of
$E,B$, and the verification below exhibits the composite map. In particular $u$
and $S$ are continuous, and the definitions use no derivative of the fields.

(c) [Pointwise reading, quadratic character] The definitions use only the values
of $E$ and $B$ at the same point $(x,t)$, and they are quadratic in the fields:
for every real $\lambda$ one has $u(\lambda E,\lambda B)=\lambda^2u(E,B)$ and
$S(\lambda E,\lambda B)=\lambda^2S(E,B)$, and $u\ge0$. Consequently
decompositions of the fields do not make $u$ or $S$ additive; cross terms
generally contribute. No convention beyond the fixed laboratory frame enters
the definitions.

(d) [Products and singular support] If $E,B$ are only locally integrable (the
weak branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]), the products $E_iE_j$, $B_iB_j$ and
the components of $E\times B$ need not be locally integrable, and no product of
distributions is defined. The displayed formulas then define $u$ and $S$
pointwise almost everywhere, and the framework uses them only where the local
integrability of the products, respectively of the component being integrated,
is separately established. No value of $u$ or $S$ is assigned at a point of
singular source support.

(e) [Status] This item defines quantities only. The interpretation of $u$ as an
energy density and of $S$ as an energy flux density, and every balance identity
involving them, is the content of [[pthm-em-poynting-balance]] and of the other
balance items of this page; no identification of $(u,S)$ with components of a
covariant tensor is made here, and the relation $S=c^2g$ to the momentum density
$g$ of [[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]] is a consequence of those definitions,
not an identification made at this point.

Retain the fields $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of [[def-em-fields]], the
energy density $u$ and Poynting vector $S$ of [[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]],
the laboratory region, its frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and its spatial
Euclidean structure of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], the constants and units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and the partial derivatives $\partial_j$ of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. Write $x=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ for the
position in the spatial chart, $\delta_{ij}$ for the Kronecker symbol
($\delta_{ij}=1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise), $\lvert E\rvert^2=\langle E,E\rangle$
with the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and
$\times$ for the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] in the frame
basis. Let $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and $\mu_0>0$ be the constants of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Momentum density] The **electromagnetic momentum density** is the map
$g:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ defined by

$$g:=\frac{S}{c^2}=\varepsilon_0\,E\times B,$$

in $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-2}\mathrm s^{-1}$; the second equality uses
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$.

(b) [Maxwell stress tensor] The **Maxwell stress tensor** is the spatial
tensor field $\sigma$ on $\Omega\times I$ with components

$$\sigma_{ij}:=\varepsilon_0\Bigl(E_iE_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\lvert E\rvert^2\Bigr)+\frac{1}{\mu_0}\Bigl(B_iB_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\lvert B\rvert^2\Bigr),$$

in $\mathrm N\,\mathrm m^{-2}=\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}$; the indices range over
$\{1,2,3\}$ and repeated symbols are not summed here, every sum being written
explicitly. The tensor is **symmetric**, $\sigma_{ij}=\sigma_{ji}$ for all
$i,j$, by inspection of the displayed expression. Its divergence is the vector
field with components
$(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i:=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_j\sigma_{ij}$, the partial
derivatives being taken at fixed $t$.

(c) [Momentum flux] The **momentum flux tensor** is $\Pi:=-\sigma$, with
$(\operatorname{div}\Pi)_i:=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_j\Pi_{ij}$; then
$\operatorname{div}\Pi=-\operatorname{div}\sigma$ componentwise.

(d) [Orbital angular momentum density and its flux] Relative to the origin of
the spatial chart, the **orbital angular momentum density** is
$\ell:=x\times g$, with components $\ell_i=\sum_{j,k=1}^{3}\epsilon_{ijk}x_jg_k$,
and its **flux tensor** is the spatial tensor field $x\times\Pi$ with
components

$$(x\times\Pi)_{i\ell}=\sum_{j,k=1}^{3}\epsilon_{ijk}\,x_j\,\Pi_{k\ell}.$$

Here $\epsilon_{ijk}$ is the Levi-Civita symbol, defined by
$\epsilon_{ijk}=+1$ if $(i,j,k)$ is an even permutation of $(1,2,3)$,
$\epsilon_{ijk}=-1$ if it is an odd permutation, and $\epsilon_{ijk}=0$ if two
indices coincide, in the positively oriented basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. The object
$\ell$ carries $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-1}\mathrm s^{-1}$ and the components
of $x\times\Pi$ carry $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm s^{-2}=\mathrm N\,\mathrm m^{-1}$.

(e) [Origin] Both $\ell$ and $x\times\Pi$ depend on the origin of the spatial
chart: under a shift $x\mapsto x+a$ of the origin by a constant $a\in\mathbb R^3$
their values become $\ell+a\times g$ and $x\times\Pi+a\times\Pi$ respectively,
so the definition fixes one origin in the laboratory frame and every statement
about $\ell$ or $x\times\Pi$ is relative to that fixed origin.

(f) [Status] This item fixes objects and index conventions only. No balance
identity and no interpretation of $\sigma$ or $\Pi$ as force or momentum flux
is asserted here; every balance identity involving these objects is the content
of the separate theorem items of this page.

(g) [Quadratic character and singular support] All five objects are quadratic
in the fields $E,B$. For a locally integrable branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] the exclusions recorded in
[[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]] apply to each of them: the products
$E_iE_j$, $B_iB_j$ and the components of $E\times B$ need not be locally
integrable, no product of distributions is defined, and the displayed formulas
then define the objects pointwise almost everywhere, the framework using them
only where the local integrability of the products is separately established.
No value is assigned at a point of singular source support.

(h) [No covariant object] No four-dimensional or covariant interpretation of
$(u,S,g,\sigma)$ is defined here; in particular $g$ is not identified with the
spatial components of a covariant momentum density.

Assume the smooth branch of the vacuum Maxwell postulate
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] on the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of
[[def-em-lab-geometry]]: the fields $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ are
jointly $C^1$ of [[def-em-fields]] and satisfy, with the continuous source
fields $\rho,J$ of [[def-em-sources]] and the constants of
[[def-em-si-conventions]],

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad\operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$$

pointwise on $\Omega\times I$, with $\operatorname{div}$ and
$\operatorname{curl}$ of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]
applied at fixed times and $\partial_t$ the partial derivative at fixed
position of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. Let $u$ and $S$ be
the energy density and Poynting vector of [[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]]. Then:

(a) [Local identity] On $\Omega\times I$,

$$\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}S=-J\cdot E,$$

where $\operatorname{div}S$ is taken at fixed time and $J\cdot E$ is the
Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

(b) [Fixed-volume identity] Let $\Omega'\subseteq\Omega$ be open with
$\overline{\Omega'}\subseteq\Omega$ carrying the finite piecewise $C^1$
presentation of
[[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-piecewise-c-one-domains]], let
$t_0<t_1$ with $(t_0,t_1)\subseteq I$, and let $n$ be the outward unit normal
of $\partial\Omega'$. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), the hypothesis under which
that divergence theorem is stated. Then for every $t\in(t_0,t_1)$,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega'}u(x,t)\,dx=-\int_{\Omega'}J\cdot E\,dx-\oint_{\partial\Omega'}S\cdot n\,dS,$$

the closed-surface integral being the finite face sum of that divergence
theorem and the derivative being the derivative of the one-variable function
$t\mapsto\int_{\Omega'}u(x,t)\,dx$ on $(t_0,t_1)$.

(c) [Interpretation and scope] Under clause (ii) of
[[post-em-lorentz-coupling]], $J\cdot E$ is the power density supplied to the
matter model of that coupling, so (a) and (b) read as a local, respectively
fixed-volume, energy balance of the field and that matter model. Nothing is
claimed for a prescribed current without such a matter model, for the weak
branch of the Maxwell postulate, for singular sources, or at field points
where the products defining $u$ or $S$ are not locally integrable; the
fixed-volume identity retains both the work term and the boundary flux. The
field-energy rate can vanish by cancellation of these two terms; vanishing
boundary flux alone does not eliminate exchange with matter. A conservation
claim for field plus matter additionally requires an explicit matter balance. This is a
conditional consequence of the adopted postulates, not an empirical claim.

Assume the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] and clause (ii) of
[[post-em-lorentz-coupling]] on the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$
of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]: the fields $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ are
jointly $C^1$ of [[def-em-fields]], the source fields $\rho,J$ are continuous
of [[def-em-sources]], the constants are those of [[def-em-si-conventions]],
the force density is
$f:=\rho E+J\times B$ of that clause (ii), in
$\mathrm N\,\mathrm m^{-3}$, and $g,\sigma,\Pi=-\sigma$ are the momentum
density, Maxwell stress and momentum flux of
[[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]]. Then:

(a) [Local identity] On $\Omega\times I$, componentwise,

$$\partial_tg-\operatorname{div}\sigma=-f,\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad\partial_tg+\operatorname{div}\Pi=-f,$$

that is, $\partial_tg_i-\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_j\sigma_{ij}=-(\rho E_i+(J\times B)_i)$ for every $i$, with $\partial_t$ the partial derivative at fixed position and $\operatorname{div}$ taken at fixed time.

(b) [Fixed-volume identity] Let $\Omega'\subseteq\Omega$ be open with
$\overline{\Omega'}\subseteq\Omega$ carrying the finite piecewise $C^1$
presentation of
[[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-piecewise-c-one-domains]], let
$t_0<t_1$ with $(t_0,t_1)\subseteq I$, assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $n$ be the outward unit normal. Then for
every $t\in(t_0,t_1)$ and every $i$,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega'}g_i\,dx=\oint_{\partial\Omega'}\Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^{3}\sigma_{ij}n_j\Bigr)dS-\int_{\Omega'}f_i\,dx=-\oint_{\partial\Omega'}\Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^{3}\Pi_{ij}n_j\Bigr)dS-\int_{\Omega'}f_i\,dx,$$

the closed-surface integrals being the finite face sums of that divergence
theorem.

(c) [Scope] The identities are conditional on the two adopted postulates. The
force density $f$ is defined only for the matter model of clause (ii), so no
claim is made about a prescribed current without such a matter model. No
conservation of field-plus-matter momentum follows without explicit matter
balances and their boundary fluxes. The field-momentum rate in (b) is the
boundary traction minus the integrated matter force; these terms can cancel,
and neither may be discarded without justification. The weak branch, singular sources and
non-integrable products are excluded as in
[[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]]; no self-force, radiation reaction or
magnetic-monopole coupling is included, in accordance with the exclusions of
[[post-em-lorentz-coupling]]. This is not an empirical claim.

Let $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, $\omega>0$ and $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$, and let
$(E,B)$ be the plane-wave fields of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]] on the
whole-space region $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$, with the terminology and
phase convention of that definition, the cross product and inner product of
[[def-cross-product-in-r3]] and [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] extended to
$\mathbb C^3$ componentwise, the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]] and
$\hat k=k/|k|$. Then:

(a) [Amplitude equations] $(E,B)$ satisfies the four smooth-branch vacuum
Maxwell equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with $\rho\equiv0$ and
$J\equiv0$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ if and only if

$$k\cdot e=0,\qquad k\cdot b=0,\qquad k\times e=\omega b,\qquad k\times b=-\frac{\omega}{c^2}e .$$

(b) [Dispersion, nonzero waves, two polarizations] The amplitude equations
admit a nonzero solution $(e,b)\ne(0,0)$ if and only if
$|k|^2=\omega^2/c^2$; off this dispersion relation the only solution is
$e=b=0$. On the dispersion relation both zero and nonzero solutions occur; a
particular solution is nonzero exactly when its amplitudes are not both zero,
in the sense of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]](c). If $|k|=\omega/c$, the
solutions are exactly the pairs $(e,b)$ with
$e\in\{v\in\mathbb C^3: k\cdot v=0\}$ arbitrary and $b=k\times e/\omega$: a
complex two-dimensional family; $e=0$ gives the zero wave, and for every
nonzero solution $e\ne0$ and $b\ne0$.

(c) [Transversality, orthogonality, magnitude relation and the wave equation]
For every solution with $|k|=\omega/c$ and every
$(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$: $k\cdot E(x,t)=k\cdot B(x,t)=0$,
$E(x,t)\cdot B(x,t)=0$ and $B(x,t)=\hat k\times E(x,t)/c$; in particular
$|B(x,t)|=|E(x,t)|/c$. Each component of $E$ and of $B$ is a $C^\infty$
solution of the wave equation $\Delta v=c^{-2}\partial_t^2v$ of
[[pthm-em-vacuum-wave-equation]] on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$.

(d) [Scope] The equivalence in (a) is between the amplitude equations and
membership in the source-free smooth Maxwell branch; it says nothing about
fields that solve the wave equations but not the amplitude equations (see
[[pthm-em-vacuum-wave-equation]](b)). The item covers ideal whole-space plane
waves only, makes no finite-energy, boundary, material or empirical claim, and
is conditional on the adopted postulate.

Fix a wavevector $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ and a positive angular
frequency $\omega>0$; here $k$ carries the unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $\omega$
the unit $\mathrm s^{-1}$ in the SI conventions of [[def-em-si-conventions]].
Fix complex amplitudes $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$, where $e$ carries the unit
$\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $b$ the unit T of the electric and magnetic
fields of [[def-em-fields]]. Let $k\cdot x$ denote the Euclidean inner product
of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and let $\exp$ and $\operatorname{Re}$ be
those of the encoding definition [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]], whose
convention that physical fields are the real parts of complex expressions is
used throughout. Define, for each $t\in\mathbb R$, maps
$E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ by

$$E(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e\,\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))\bigr),\qquad B(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(b\,\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))\bigr),$$

componentwise, and put $|k|:=\sqrt{\langle k,k\rangle}$,
$\hat k:=k/|k|$ and $T:=2\pi/\omega$. Terminology: $k$ is the **wavevector**,
$\hat k$ the **propagation direction**, $|k|$ the **wavenumber**, $\omega$ the
**angular frequency**, $T$ the **period**, $e,b$ the **complex amplitudes**,
and $\theta(x,t):=k\cdot x-\omega t$ the **phase**. Then:

(a) [Objects, domain and regularity] Both maps are of class $C^\infty$ on
$\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, as verified below; on the whole-space laboratory region
$\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] they are an
electric and a magnetic field of [[def-em-fields]] of every finite class
$C^k$, $k\ge1$, read in the frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$.

(b) [Phase and periodicity] At fixed $x$ the map $t\mapsto\theta(x,t)$ is
affine with derivative $-\omega<0$, so the phase decreases in time (the
$e^{-i\omega t}$ convention); $E$ and $B$ depend on $(x,t)$ only through
$\theta$ and are $T$-periodic in $t$.

(c) [Zero and nonzero waves] $(E,B)$ is the identically zero pair on
$\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ if and only if $e=b=0$; call the wave
**nonzero** otherwise. The electric field alone determines $e$ and the
magnetic field alone determines $b$, because
$\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\theta})=0$ for all real $\theta$ forces $w=0$
(evaluate at $\theta=0$ and at $\theta=\pi/2$).

(d) [Status] This item fixes objects, conventions and terminology only. It
asserts no field equation, no dispersion relation, no transversality, no
energy claim and no polarization classification; those are the content of
[[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]] and [[def-em-polarization-definition]]. The
units and the propagation constant $c$ are those of
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and no empirical realization or measurement is
claimed.

### Well-definedness and conventions

For every $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ the phase $\theta(x,t)$ is a
real number, so $i\theta(x,t)$ is a complex number and
$\exp(i\theta(x,t))$ is defined by the everywhere-convergent exponential
series of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]]; multiplying by the complex number
$e_j$ or $b_j$ and taking real parts is likewise defined, so each $E_j$ and
$B_j$ is a well-defined real-valued function. Since $\omega>0$ and $k\ne0$,
$T=2\pi/\omega>0$ and $|k|>0$, so $\hat k$ is defined. The joint map
$(x,t)\mapsto(E(x,t),B(x,t))$ has the open set $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$
as its domain. For regularity, let $q=(k_1,k_2,k_3,-\omega)$ and
$y=(x_1,x_2,x_3,t)$. The exponential has derivative itself
([[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]), its complex
derivative is also its real total derivative
([[thm-complex-differentiability-real-linearity-wirtinger-and-cauchy-riemann]]),
and the real-linear map $\operatorname{Re}$ commutes with differentiation by
[[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]. Thus for every coordinate word
$(j_1,\ldots,j_m)$ and component $\ell$,
$\partial_{y_{j_m}}\cdots\partial_{y_{j_1}}E_\ell
=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e_\ell\prod_{r=1}^m(iq_{j_r})\exp(iq\cdot y)\bigr)$,
by induction using the same chain rule; the identical formula holds with
$b_\ell$ for $B_\ell$. These expressions are continuous for every finite
word, proving the $C^\infty$ assertion in (a).
The equivalence in (c) is the elementary injectivity of
$w\mapsto\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\cdot})$ on $\mathbb C^3$: if
$\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\theta})=0$ for every real $\theta$, then taking
$\theta=0$ gives $\operatorname{Re}w=0$ and taking $\theta=\pi/2$ gives
$\operatorname{Re}(iw)=-\operatorname{Im}w=0$, so $w=0$, and the converse is
immediate. The complex notation is an encoding of real fields and of real
linear equations, not a complex physical field; the symbols $e$ and $b$ are
constant complex amplitudes, not fields. No electromagnetic equation, no
matter model and no physical interpretation is introduced by this
definition; in particular the complex amplitudes need not satisfy the
Maxwell amplitude equations, and the plane-wave expressions above are
defined for every $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.
For all $u,v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product is bilinear and alternating, $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$, and $u\times v$ is orthogonal to both $u$ and $v$.

For $u,v\in\mathbb R^3$, $\|u\times v\|_2^2=\det G(u,v)$, and this value is positive exactly when $u$ and $v$ are linearly independent.

Equivalently,
$$\|u\times v\|_2^2=\|u\|_2^2\|v\|_2^2-\langle u,v\rangle^2.$$

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. For $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $a_j\le b_j$ for $j<m$, define
$$[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\},\qquad \operatorname{vol}[a,b]:=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j).$$
The product is the recursively defined finite product of [[def-finite-sum]]. The rectangle is **nondegenerate** when every $a_j<b_j$, and it is a **cube** when all side lengths are equal.

Every factor is nonnegative, so volume is nonnegative. For a coordinate index $r<m$, cutting at $c\in[a_r,b_r]$ gives two rectangles whose volumes add to the original, by distributivity in that factor and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Under the standard identification $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]), this is the interval $[a_0,b_0]$ and its length.

For a bounded function $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ on a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, define
$$\underline{\int_Q}f:=\sup_P L(f,P),\qquad \overline{\int_Q}f:=\inf_P U(f,P),$$
over all grid partitions $P$ of $Q$. The grid family is nonempty, since the endpoints in each coordinate give a one-cell grid. Every lower sum is at most every upper sum by a common refinement and [[lem-multidimensional-refinement-inequalities]], so the two sets of sums are nonempty and bounded and the extrema exist ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-unique]]).

The function is **Riemann integrable over $Q$** when the two values agree.
Their unique common real is $\int_Q f$. No integral is defined here for a
degenerate rectangle, because the grid definition requires every coordinate
interval to have distinct endpoints. This is the multidimensional Darboux
definition; its agreement with the published one-dimensional definition is
proved separately.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

derivations.claim: Setup and componentwise averages. Fix $x\in\mathbb R^3$ and put $\alpha:=e\,e^{ik\cdot x}$, $\delta:=b\,e^{ik\cdot x}\in\mathbb C^3$, so that $E_i=\operatorname{Re}(\alpha_ie^{-i\omega t})$ and $B_i=\operatorname{Re}(\delta_ie^{-i\omega t})$ for each $i$ by [F6], with $\theta=k\cdot x-\omega t$. Applying the scalar and vector forms of [F1] with $a=\alpha$, $d=\alpha$; $a=\delta$, $d=\delta$; and the cross-product form with $a=\alpha$, $d=\delta$, and using $\alpha_i\overline{\alpha_j}=e_ie^{ik\cdot x}\overline{e_j}e^{-ik\cdot x}=e_i\overline{e_j}$ and $|\alpha_i|^2=|e_i|^2$, gives $\langle E_iE_j\rangle=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(e_i\overline{e_j})$, $\langle B_iB_j\rangle=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(b_i\overline{b_j})$ and $\langle E\times B\rangle=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(e\times\overline b)$, and $\langle|E|^2\rangle=\frac12|e|^2$, $\langle|B|^2\rangle=\frac12|b|^2$, all independent of the starting time and of $x$.

Clause (a). By [F2] and step 1.1, $\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\langle|E|^2\rangle+\frac{1}{2\mu_0}\langle|B|^2\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{4}|e|^2+\frac{1}{4\mu_0}|b|^2$. Write $e=a+id$ with $a,d\in\mathbb R^3$. Since $k$ is real and $k\cdot e=0$, both $k\cdot a$ and $k\cdot d$ vanish. The real Gram identity of [F8] applied separately to $a$ and $d$ gives $|b|^2=(|k\times a|^2+|k\times d|^2)/\omega^2=|k|^2(|a|^2+|d|^2)/\omega^2=|e|^2/c^2$ because $|k|=\omega/c$; hence $\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{4}|e|^2+\frac{\varepsilon_0}{4}|e|^2=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}|e|^2$ by $1/(\mu_0c^2)=\varepsilon_0$ of [F10]. The value is independent of $x$ (the phase factors cancel in step 1.1) and of the starting time: the integrand is $T$-periodic and continuous, so its integral over any interval of length $T$ equals $\int_0^T$ by [F7] applied to the function $G(s)=\int_s^{s+T}f$ with $G'=0$.

Clause (b). By [F2] and the cross-product average of step 1.1, $\langle S\rangle=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\langle E\times B\rangle=\frac{1}{2\mu_0}\operatorname{Re}(e\times\overline b)$. Since $b=k\times e/\omega$ and $k$ is real, $e\times\overline b=\frac1\omega e\times(k\times\overline e)=\frac1\omega\bigl[k\langle e,\overline e\rangle-\overline e\langle e,k\rangle\bigr]=\frac1\omega k|e|^2$ by the triple-product identity of [F8] and $\langle e,k\rangle=0$; hence $\langle S\rangle=\frac{|e|^2}{2\mu_0\omega}k=\frac{|e|^2|k|}{2\mu_0\omega}\hat k=\frac{|e|^2}{2\mu_0c}\hat k=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|e|^2\hat k$ by $|k|=\omega/c$ and $1/(\mu_0c)=\varepsilon_0c$ of [F10]. Comparing with step 2.1 gives $\langle S\rangle=\langle u\rangle c\hat k$ and $I=|\langle S\rangle|=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|e|^2=c\langle u\rangle$.

Clause (c), tensor identity. By [F3] and step 1.1, $\langle\sigma_{ij}\rangle=\varepsilon_0\bigl(\frac12\operatorname{Re}(e_i\overline{e_j})-\frac14\delta_{ij}|e|^2\bigr)+\frac{1}{\mu_0}\bigl(\frac12\operatorname{Re}(b_i\overline{b_j})-\frac14\delta_{ij}|b|^2\bigr)$. For the magnetic term, the coordinate identity of [F8] for the cross product applied componentwise gives $\operatorname{Re}(b_i\overline{b_j})=\frac{1}{\omega^2}\operatorname{Re}\bigl[(k\times e)_i\overline{(k\times e)_j}\bigr]=\frac{1}{\omega^2}\bigl[|k|^2|e|^2\delta_{ij}-k_ik_j|e|^2-|k|^2\operatorname{Re}(e_i\overline{e_j})\bigr]$: multiplying the coordinate formula for $(k\times e)_i$ and $\overline{(k\times e)_j}$ and summing over the repeated indices leaves exactly the three displayed contractions, using $\langle k,e\rangle=0$ and the reality of $k$, and $\operatorname{Re}(\overline{e_i}e_j)=\operatorname{Re}(e_i\overline{e_j})$ by [F9]. Substituting, the two $\operatorname{Re}(e_i\overline{e_j})$ coefficients are $\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}-\frac{|k|^2}{2\mu_0\omega^2}=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}-\frac{1}{2\mu_0c^2}=0$ by $|k|^2/\omega^2=1/c^2$ and [F10], and the total $\delta_{ij}$ contribution is $-\frac{\varepsilon_0}{4}|e|^2+\frac{|k|^2|e|^2}{2\mu_0\omega^2}-\frac{1}{4\mu_0}|b|^2=(-\frac{\varepsilon_0}{4}+\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}-\frac{\varepsilon_0}{4})|e|^2=0$ using $|b|^2=|e|^2/c^2$ from step 2.1; there remains $\langle\sigma_{ij}\rangle=-\frac{|k|^2|e|^2}{2\mu_0\omega^2}\frac{k_ik_j}{|k|^2}=-\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}|e|^2\hat k_i\hat k_j=-\langle u\rangle\hat k_i\hat k_j$ by [F10] and step 2.1, so $\langle\Pi_{ij}\rangle=-\langle\sigma_{ij}\rangle=\langle u\rangle\hat k_i\hat k_j$.

citations.quote:
Assume the vacuum Maxwell postulate [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] on the laboratory
region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the fields of
[[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]], and fix the constants
$\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ of
[[def-em-si-conventions]]. Let $n\ge1$, let
$(E_1,B_1,\rho_1,J_1),\dots,(E_n,B_n,\rho_n,J_n)$ be $n$ field-source pairs
each satisfying one and the same branch of the postulate on the same region
(all in the smooth branch, or all in the weak branch), and let
$a_1,\dots,a_n\in\mathbb R$. Put $E:=\sum_{j=1}^na_jE_j$,
$B:=\sum_{j=1}^na_jB_j$, $\rho:=\sum_{j=1}^na_j\rho_j$ and
$J:=\sum_{j=1}^na_jJ_j$. Then:

(a) $(E,B,\rho,J)$ satisfies the same branch of the postulate on the same
region with the same constants: pointwise in the smooth branch and in the sense
of the pairings of clause (b) of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] in the weak branch.

(b) Nothing beyond this linearity is asserted: the result does not apply to a
source whose density depends nonlinearly on the fields (a nonlinear
constitutive law), and no convergence statement is made for infinite series or
integrals of solutions or for infinite linear combinations.

(c) The theorem is conditional on the adopted postulate and is not an empirical
claim about nature.

Let $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, $\omega>0$ and $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$, and let
$(E,B)$ be the plane-wave fields of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]] on the
whole-space region $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$, with the terminology and
phase convention of that definition, the cross product and inner product of
[[def-cross-product-in-r3]] and [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] extended to
$\mathbb C^3$ componentwise, the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]] and
$\hat k=k/|k|$. Then:

(a) [Amplitude equations] $(E,B)$ satisfies the four smooth-branch vacuum
Maxwell equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with $\rho\equiv0$ and
$J\equiv0$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ if and only if

$$k\cdot e=0,\qquad k\cdot b=0,\qquad k\times e=\omega b,\qquad k\times b=-\frac{\omega}{c^2}e .$$

(b) [Dispersion, nonzero waves, two polarizations] The amplitude equations
admit a nonzero solution $(e,b)\ne(0,0)$ if and only if
$|k|^2=\omega^2/c^2$; off this dispersion relation the only solution is
$e=b=0$. On the dispersion relation both zero and nonzero solutions occur; a
particular solution is nonzero exactly when its amplitudes are not both zero,
in the sense of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]](c). If $|k|=\omega/c$, the
solutions are exactly the pairs $(e,b)$ with
$e\in\{v\in\mathbb C^3: k\cdot v=0\}$ arbitrary and $b=k\times e/\omega$: a
complex two-dimensional family; $e=0$ gives the zero wave, and for every
nonzero solution $e\ne0$ and $b\ne0$.

(c) [Transversality, orthogonality, magnitude relation and the wave equation]
For every solution with $|k|=\omega/c$ and every
$(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$: $k\cdot E(x,t)=k\cdot B(x,t)=0$,
$E(x,t)\cdot B(x,t)=0$ and $B(x,t)=\hat k\times E(x,t)/c$; in particular
$|B(x,t)|=|E(x,t)|/c$. Each component of $E$ and of $B$ is a $C^\infty$
solution of the wave equation $\Delta v=c^{-2}\partial_t^2v$ of
[[pthm-em-vacuum-wave-equation]] on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$.

(d) [Scope] The equivalence in (a) is between the amplitude equations and
membership in the source-free smooth Maxwell branch; it says nothing about
fields that solve the wave equations but not the amplitude equations (see
[[pthm-em-vacuum-wave-equation]](b)). The item covers ideal whole-space plane
waves only, makes no finite-energy, boundary, material or empirical claim, and
is conditional on the adopted postulate.

Fix a wavevector $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ and a positive angular
frequency $\omega>0$; here $k$ carries the unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $\omega$
the unit $\mathrm s^{-1}$ in the SI conventions of [[def-em-si-conventions]].
Fix complex amplitudes $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$, where $e$ carries the unit
$\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $b$ the unit T of the electric and magnetic
fields of [[def-em-fields]]. Let $k\cdot x$ denote the Euclidean inner product
of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and let $\exp$ and $\operatorname{Re}$ be
those of the encoding definition [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]], whose
convention that physical fields are the real parts of complex expressions is
used throughout. Define, for each $t\in\mathbb R$, maps
$E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ by

$$E(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e\,\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))\bigr),\qquad B(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(b\,\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))\bigr),$$

componentwise, and put $|k|:=\sqrt{\langle k,k\rangle}$,
$\hat k:=k/|k|$ and $T:=2\pi/\omega$. Terminology: $k$ is the **wavevector**,
$\hat k$ the **propagation direction**, $|k|$ the **wavenumber**, $\omega$ the
**angular frequency**, $T$ the **period**, $e,b$ the **complex amplitudes**,
and $\theta(x,t):=k\cdot x-\omega t$ the **phase**. Then:

(a) [Objects, domain and regularity] Both maps are of class $C^\infty$ on
$\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, as verified below; on the whole-space laboratory region
$\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] they are an
electric and a magnetic field of [[def-em-fields]] of every finite class
$C^k$, $k\ge1$, read in the frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$.

(b) [Phase and periodicity] At fixed $x$ the map $t\mapsto\theta(x,t)$ is
affine with derivative $-\omega<0$, so the phase decreases in time (the
$e^{-i\omega t}$ convention); $E$ and $B$ depend on $(x,t)$ only through
$\theta$ and are $T$-periodic in $t$.

(c) [Zero and nonzero waves] $(E,B)$ is the identically zero pair on
$\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ if and only if $e=b=0$; call the wave
**nonzero** otherwise. The electric field alone determines $e$ and the
magnetic field alone determines $b$, because
$\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\theta})=0$ for all real $\theta$ forces $w=0$
(evaluate at $\theta=0$ and at $\theta=\pi/2$).

(d) [Status] This item fixes objects, conventions and terminology only. It
asserts no field equation, no dispersion relation, no transversality, no
energy claim and no polarization classification; those are the content of
[[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]] and [[def-em-polarization-definition]]. The
units and the propagation constant $c$ are those of
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and no empirical realization or measurement is
claimed.

### Well-definedness and conventions

For every $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ the phase $\theta(x,t)$ is a
real number, so $i\theta(x,t)$ is a complex number and
$\exp(i\theta(x,t))$ is defined by the everywhere-convergent exponential
series of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]]; multiplying by the complex number
$e_j$ or $b_j$ and taking real parts is likewise defined, so each $E_j$ and
$B_j$ is a well-defined real-valued function. Since $\omega>0$ and $k\ne0$,
$T=2\pi/\omega>0$ and $|k|>0$, so $\hat k$ is defined. The joint map
$(x,t)\mapsto(E(x,t),B(x,t))$ has the open set $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$
as its domain. For regularity, let $q=(k_1,k_2,k_3,-\omega)$ and
$y=(x_1,x_2,x_3,t)$. The exponential has derivative itself
([[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]), its complex
derivative is also its real total derivative
([[thm-complex-differentiability-real-linearity-wirtinger-and-cauchy-riemann]]),
and the real-linear map $\operatorname{Re}$ commutes with differentiation by
[[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]. Thus for every coordinate word
$(j_1,\ldots,j_m)$ and component $\ell$,
$\partial_{y_{j_m}}\cdots\partial_{y_{j_1}}E_\ell
=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e_\ell\prod_{r=1}^m(iq_{j_r})\exp(iq\cdot y)\bigr)$,
by induction using the same chain rule; the identical formula holds with
$b_\ell$ for $B_\ell$. These expressions are continuous for every finite
word, proving the $C^\infty$ assertion in (a).
The equivalence in (c) is the elementary injectivity of
$w\mapsto\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\cdot})$ on $\mathbb C^3$: if
$\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\theta})=0$ for every real $\theta$, then taking
$\theta=0$ gives $\operatorname{Re}w=0$ and taking $\theta=\pi/2$ gives
$\operatorname{Re}(iw)=-\operatorname{Im}w=0$, so $w=0$, and the converse is
immediate. The complex notation is an encoding of real fields and of real
linear equations, not a complex physical field; the symbols $e$ and $b$ are
constant complex amplitudes, not fields. No electromagnetic equation, no
matter model and no physical interpretation is introduced by this
definition; in particular the complex amplitudes need not satisfy the
Maxwell amplitude equations, and the plane-wave expressions above are
defined for every $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$.

Let $\omega>0$ and $T:=2\pi/\omega>0$.

**Scalar form.** Let $a,d\in\mathbb C$. Then

$$\frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}\bigl(ae^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\operatorname{Re}\bigl(de^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}\bigl(a\overline d\bigr).$$

**Vector forms.** Let $a,d\in\mathbb C^3$, write the same symbols for the componentwise complex-bilinear extensions of the Euclidean inner product and of the cross product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] to $\mathbb C^3$, and let $\operatorname{Re}$ act componentwise. In coordinate formulas, $\epsilon_{ijk}$ is $+1$ for even permutations of $(1,2,3)$, $-1$ for odd permutations and zero for repeated indices; all displayed repeated-index sums run from 1 to 3. Then

$$\frac1T\int_0^T\bigl\langle\operatorname{Re}\bigl(ae^{-i\omega t}\bigr),\operatorname{Re}\bigl(de^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\bigr\rangle\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\langle a,\overline d\rangle\bigr),\qquad \frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}\bigl(ae^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\times\operatorname{Re}\bigl(de^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}\bigl(a\times\overline d\bigr),$$

the integrals of the real vector-valued integrands being componentwise. The real-valued functions $\operatorname{Re}(ae^{-i\omega t})$ are the time-dependent factors of the plane-wave fields of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]] at a fixed position, with the phase absorbed into $a$ and $d$; no electromagnetic interpretation is asserted. Real quadratic expressions may not be replaced by complex quadratic expressions without conjugation: the average is not $\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(ad)$ in general. For $a=d=1+i$ the proved average is $\tfrac12|1+i|^2=1$, whereas $\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}((1+i)^2)=0$.

Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], so
that $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a nonempty open interval, $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$
is nonempty open, $x=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ is the position in the spatial chart,
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the frame basis of the spatial slice, and the spatial inner
product is the Euclidean form $\delta$; let the units and the constants $c>0$,
$\mu_0>0$ and $\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ be those of
[[def-em-si-conventions]]; let $k\ge1$, and let
$E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be an electric and a magnetic field of class
$C^k$ of [[def-em-fields]]. Write $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ and $|\cdot|$ for
the Euclidean inner product and norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and
$\times$ for the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].

(a) [Energy density and flux] The **electromagnetic energy density**
$u:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ and the **energy flux density** (the **Poynting
vector**) $S:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ are defined by

$$u(x,t):=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\,\langle E(x,t),E(x,t)\rangle+\frac{1}{2\mu_0}\,\langle B(x,t),B(x,t)\rangle,\qquad S(x,t):=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\,E(x,t)\times B(x,t).$$

At fixed $t\in I$ the map $u(\cdot,t):\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is a real-valued
function on $\Omega$ and $S(\cdot,t):\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ is a spatial vector
field on $\Omega$, read in the basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. The energy density
carries $\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}=\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-1}\mathrm s^{-2}$ and
the energy flux density carries $\mathrm W\,\mathrm m^{-2}=\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm s^{-3}$.

(b) [Regularity] If $E,B$ are of class $C^k$, then $u$ and $S$ are of class
$C^k$: they are the components of a polynomial expression in the components of
$E,B$, and the verification below exhibits the composite map. In particular $u$
and $S$ are continuous, and the definitions use no derivative of the fields.

(c) [Pointwise reading, quadratic character] The definitions use only the values
of $E$ and $B$ at the same point $(x,t)$, and they are quadratic in the fields:
for every real $\lambda$ one has $u(\lambda E,\lambda B)=\lambda^2u(E,B)$ and
$S(\lambda E,\lambda B)=\lambda^2S(E,B)$, and $u\ge0$. Consequently
decompositions of the fields do not make $u$ or $S$ additive; cross terms
generally contribute. No convention beyond the fixed laboratory frame enters
the definitions.

(d) [Products and singular support] If $E,B$ are only locally integrable (the
weak branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]), the products $E_iE_j$, $B_iB_j$ and
the components of $E\times B$ need not be locally integrable, and no product of
distributions is defined. The displayed formulas then define $u$ and $S$
pointwise almost everywhere, and the framework uses them only where the local
integrability of the products, respectively of the component being integrated,
is separately established. No value of $u$ or $S$ is assigned at a point of
singular source support.

(e) [Status] This item defines quantities only. The interpretation of $u$ as an
energy density and of $S$ as an energy flux density, and every balance identity
involving them, is the content of [[pthm-em-poynting-balance]] and of the other
balance items of this page; no identification of $(u,S)$ with components of a
covariant tensor is made here, and the relation $S=c^2g$ to the momentum density
$g$ of [[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]] is a consequence of those definitions,
not an identification made at this point.

Let $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, $\omega>0$ with $\omega=c|k|$, let
$e\in\mathbb C^3$ with $k\cdot e=0$ and $b=k\times e/\omega$, and let $(E,B)$ be
the corresponding plane-wave solution of [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]]
([[def-em-plane-wave-definition]]) on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$. Let $u$ and
$S$ be the energy density and Poynting vector of
[[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]], and $g=S/c^2$, $\sigma$, $\Pi=-\sigma$ the
momentum density, Maxwell stress and momentum flux of
[[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]]. Write $T=2\pi/\omega$,
$|e|^2=e\cdot\overline e$, $\hat k=k/|k|$, and let
$\langle f\rangle:=\frac1T\int_0^Tf(x,s)\,ds$ be the period average at fixed
$x$. Then, for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$:

(a) [Averaged energy density] $\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}|e|^2$,
independent of $x$ and of the starting time.

(b) [Averaged Poynting vector]
$\langle S\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|e|^2\hat k$; hence
$\langle S\rangle=\langle u\rangle c\hat k$, and the period-averaged intensity
is $I:=|\langle S\rangle|=c\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|e|^2$.

(c) [Averaged momentum density, stress and momentum flux]
$\langle g\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2c}|e|^2\hat k$, and componentwise
$\langle\sigma_{ij}\rangle=-\langle u\rangle\hat k_i\hat k_j$, equivalently
$\langle\Pi_{ij}\rangle=\langle u\rangle\hat k_i\hat k_j$; the period-averaged
momentum flux across a plane with unit normal $n$ is therefore
$\langle u\rangle(\hat k\cdot n)\hat k$, a pure flux along $\hat k$ with signed
coefficient $(I/c)(\hat k\cdot n)$ and magnitude $(I/c)|\hat k\cdot n|$. The
tensor identity holds for every complex transverse amplitude $e$, not only for
real or circular ones.

(d) [Balance reading] On the source-free region the local identities of
[[pthm-em-poynting-balance]] and [[pthm-em-momentum-balance]] hold for this
field; since $u,g,S,\sigma$ are $T$-periodic in $t$, the period averages of
their time derivatives vanish ([[thm-ftc-second-part]]), so averaging the
identities gives $\operatorname{div}\langle S\rangle=0$ and
$\operatorname{div}\langle\sigma\rangle=0$ consistently (both averaged fields
are in fact constant), and the reading of $u,S,g,\Pi$ as energy and momentum
densities and fluxes is that of those two theorems.

(e) [Scope] These are exact identities for the ideal plane wave; $I$ is the
intensity used by the radiation-pressure thought experiment of the companion
page and in radiation-flux arguments. No detection statistics, no finite-beam
or finite-time realisation and no empirical claim is made, and the zero
amplitude gives the zero wave and zero total energy, whereas every nonzero
amplitude gives infinite total energy over $\mathbb R^3$.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

derivations.claim: Setting. For $j=1,2$ the data satisfy $|k_j|=\omega/c$, $k_j\cdot e_j=0$ and $b_j=k_j\times e_j/\omega$, so by [F2] each $(E_j,B_j)$ of [F3] is a $C^\infty$ source-free solution of the smooth vacuum Maxwell branch on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$; put $\theta_j(x,t)=k_j\cdot x-\omega t$ and $\delta(x):=(k_2-k_1)\cdot x=\theta_2(x,t)-\theta_1(x,t)$, a function of $x$ alone.

Clause (a). The pairs $(E_1,B_1,\rho_1,J_1)$ and $(E_2,B_2,\rho_2,J_2)$ with $\rho_1=\rho_2=0$, $J_1=J_2=0$ each satisfy the smooth branch on the same whole-space region by step 1.1, so [F1](a) with $n=2$ and the real coefficients $a_1,a_2$ gives that $(E,B)=a_1(E_1,B_1)+a_2(E_2,B_2)$ satisfies the smooth source-free branch with the same constants, and the fields are $C^\infty$ as finite linear combinations of $C^\infty$ fields. The single-phase rewriting follows from $\exp(i\theta_2)=\exp(i\delta(x))\exp(i\theta_1)$ and the $\mathbb R$-linearity of $\operatorname{Re}$ of [F8]: componentwise $E=\operatorname{Re}(e_1e^{i\theta_1})a_1+\operatorname{Re}(e_2e^{i\theta_1}e^{i\delta})a_2=\operatorname{Re}\bigl((a_1e_1+a_2e_2e^{i\delta})e^{i\theta_1}\bigr)=\operatorname{Re}(\alpha e^{i\theta_1})$ by the field arithmetic of $\mathbb C$, and identically for $B$ with $\beta=a_1b_1+a_2b_2e^{i\delta}$.

Clause (b). Fix $x$ and write $\theta=\theta_1(x,t)=k_1\cdot x-\omega t$, so that by step 2.1 $E=\operatorname{Re}(A e^{-i\omega t})$ and $B=\operatorname{Re}(D e^{-i\omega t})$, where $A:=\alpha(x)e^{ik_1\cdot x}$ and $D:=\beta(x)e^{ik_1\cdot x}$. Applying [F4] to the scalar components (equivalently its vector form with one component retained) gives $\langle E_iE_j\rangle=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(A_i\overline{A_j})=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(\alpha_i\overline{\alpha_j})$, since $e^{ik_1\cdot x}e^{-ik_1\cdot x}=1$, hence $\langle|E|^2\rangle=\frac12|\alpha|^2$, and likewise $\langle|B|^2\rangle=\frac12|\beta|^2$; therefore $\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{4}|\alpha|^2+\frac{1}{4\mu_0}|\beta|^2$ by [F5]. Expanding the squares with the complex bilinearity of [F7] and [F8] gives $|\alpha|^2=a_1^2|e_1|^2+a_2^2|e_2|^2+2a_1a_2\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e_1\cdot\overline e_2e^{-i\delta}\bigr)$ and $|\beta|^2=a_1^2|b_1|^2+a_2^2|b_2|^2+2a_1a_2\operatorname{Re}\bigl(b_1\cdot\overline b_2e^{-i\delta}\bigr)$. For the magnetic terms, $|b_j|^2=\omega^{-2}\langle k_j\times e_j,\overline{k_j\times e_j}\rangle=\omega^{-2}|k_j|^2|e_j|^2=|e_j|^2/c^2$ by [F7] and $k_j\cdot e_j=0$, and $b_1\cdot\overline b_2=\omega^{-2}(k_1\times e_1)\cdot\overline{(k_2\times e_2)}=\frac{|k_1||k_2|}{\omega^2}(\hat k_1\times e_1)\cdot(\hat k_2\times\overline e_2)=\frac{1}{c^2}(\hat k_1\times e_1)\cdot(\hat k_2\times\overline e_2)$; substituting and using $\frac{1}{4\mu_0c^2}=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{4}$ from the SI relation gives $\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}(a_1^2|e_1|^2+a_2^2|e_2|^2)+\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}a_1a_2\operatorname{Re}(W)$ with $W=(e_1\cdot\overline e_2+(\hat k_1\times e_1)\cdot(\hat k_2\times\overline e_2))e^{-i\delta}$, which is clause (b).

Clause (c). At the same fixed $x$, the cross-product form of [F4] gives $\langle E\times B\rangle=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(A\times\overline D)=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(\alpha\times\overline\beta)$, since the common spatial phase cancels, so $\langle S\rangle=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\langle E\times B\rangle=\frac{1}{2\mu_0}\operatorname{Re}(\alpha\times\overline\beta)$ by [F5], which is the first display of clause (c). If $k_1=k_2=:k$ then $\delta=0$, $\alpha=a_1e_1+a_2e_2=:\tilde e$ and $\beta=a_1b_1+a_2b_2$; by the bilinearity of the cross product [F7], $\beta=k\times(a_1e_1+a_2e_2)/\omega=k\times\tilde e/\omega$, and $k\cdot\tilde e=0$, so $(E,B)$ is exactly the single plane wave with amplitude $\tilde e$ and wavevector $k$, of the class covered by [F6]; clause (a) of [F6] gives $\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}|\tilde e|^2$ and clause (b) gives $\langle S\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|\tilde e|^2\hat k$. These agree with clauses (b) and the first display of (c): when $k_1=k_2=k$ the bracket in $W$ reduces to $2e_1\cdot\overline e_2$ by the identity of [F7], and $|\tilde e|^2=a_1^2|e_1|^2+a_2^2|e_2|^2+2a_1a_2\operatorname{Re}(e_1\cdot\overline e_2)$ by [F8].

Conclusion and scope. Step 2.1 is clause (a), step 3.1 is clause (b), step 3.2 is clause (c), and clause (d) is a scope qualification on the same computation: every average above is the deterministic period average at a fixed point of the specified coherent superposition, no ensemble or random-phase average, detector model, finite-sample frequency or visibility estimate is introduced, and nothing in the proof uses any property distinguishing classical from quantum descriptions of light beyond the adopted Maxwell equations and the definitions; in particular classical electromagnetic waves interfere, so these formulas do not by themselves discriminate between descriptions. The identities are conditional on the adopted postulate and make no empirical claim.
